newsitem.title: ITALY: Scepticism abounds at NGO food forum in Rome.
newsitem.headline: Scepticism abounds at NGO food forum in Rome.

text.p: When the man responsible for organising this week's World Food Summit addressed a parallel conference of non-governmental organisations on Monday, he spoke of working together towards a common goal of eradicating hunger.

Delegates to the NGO Forum applauded politely the speech by U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) director-general Jacques Diouf, but in interviews later said they believed the summit would not bring the world closer to realising that goal.
"I don't expect much from the official summit. It won't eradicate hunger," said Viplab Halin of the Calcutta, India-based Institute for Motivating Self-Employment.
"There are some very nice things written in the (summit's) Declaration but it's wishful thinking," he said. "What we need is the political will to put it into practice."
The five-day World Food Summit opens on Wednesday at the Rome headquarters of FAO. The agency says about 100 heads of state and government are expected.
A non-binding Declaration on World Food Security and a Plan of Action have already been drafted ahead of the summit for the participants to adopt without further discussion or revision.

Advocates attending the NGO Forum, which opened on Monday and which will present its own statement to the official summit, said they were frustrated that work on the summit's documents had been completed in advance.

"It's unfair. We all have to have input," said Neil Stevens, who represents a group of non-governmental organisations from the South Pacific. "We are thinking of approaching some of the heads of state on a personal level to get our views across."

Other NGO delegates took offense with the actual wording of the Declaration and Plan of Action. What particularly angered them was a decision not to enshrine "the right to food for all" in the documents.
Some rich countries like the United States had been opposed to the phrase because they were concerned it could lead to lawsuits demanding aid or special trade provisions.

The final draft instead reaffirms "the right of everyone to have access to safe and nutritious food, consistent with the right to adequate food and the fundamental right of everyone to be free from hunger".

Canadian David MacDonald, chairman of the Global Network on Food Security, said the documents were "watered down...rather than striving for the highest common goal, they have gone for the largest common denominator".
"There was a lot of unwillingness to get specific," he said.

"I can understand why some developed countries, like my own, might have some concerns, but the developing countries which are in the majority should have pushed harder. I don't see how leaders of some countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America can sign those documents," MacDonald said.
"I don't think that with these official compromises we can change anything," said Amelia Zambeze of the Mozambique Association for Rural Women.
